demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Layla

Layla was thirty-one when she arrived at the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, her hands trembling as she filled out the intake form. She worked as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm, a job she had held for four years before the accident, though she was not sure she would hold it much longer. Three years had passed since the evening that had fractured her life, and in that time she had come to believe that she was no longer the person she had been—that something fundamental inside her had broken and would never mend.

The accident had occurred on a summer evening in 2021, when Layla was driving her younger cousin Yasmin home from a family gathering. Yasmin was sixteen, sitting in the passenger seat, singing along to music on the radio. Layla had been thinking about her marriage, which was deteriorating, and her attention had drifted from the road. A child's ball had rolled into the street from between two parked cars. Layla had swerved, overcorrected, and struck a cyclist coming the opposite direction. The sound of impact—a dull, terrible crunch—had been followed by silence, and then screaming. The smell of hot asphalt mixed with something metallic and organic that she could never quite name but would never forget. The cyclist, a man in his sixties, had sustained a compound fracture of his left leg and a traumatic brain injury. He had spent six weeks in intensive care. He had recovered, but not fully. He walked with a cane now and had lost some of his memory.

Layla had not been charged criminally—the police investigation concluded it was an accident—but the internal verdict she had rendered was far harsher. In the months that followed, she became convinced that she could not be trusted, that some essential capacity for judgment or care had been absent in her that night and would remain absent. She had come to see herself as someone fundamentally unsafe, someone whose presence in the world posed a risk to others. This belief had spread like a stain across her understanding of everything she did.

At work, she had begun to avoid making decisions. Her role required her to develop social media strategies, to recommend content, to guide clients toward certain choices. But Layla found herself paralyzed by the conviction that whatever she suggested would be wrong, that her judgment was corrupted. She would sit at her desk for hours, staring at her screen, unable to commit to a recommendation. Her manager had begun to notice. There had been a performance review six months ago in which he had asked if everything was all right. She had said it was, but she was no longer sure how much longer she could sustain the pretense.

Her body had become a source of constant alarm. When a colleague leaned over her shoulder to look at her monitor, Layla would flinch violently, her heart racing as if she had been struck. When her ex-husband had called last month to discuss the divorce settlement, she had misheard something he said and had convinced herself, for a panicked moment, that Yasmin had been in an accident. These false alarms came frequently now—a car horn would sound, and Layla would be certain something terrible was happening; a notification on her phone would appear, and she would brace for catastrophic news.

What was most disturbing to her was the quality of her memories. Sometimes she could recall the exact sequence of events—the ball, the swerve, the impact—with crystalline clarity, but the memory felt as though it belonged to someone else, a story she had been told rather than something she had lived. Other times, she knew it had happened, knew it intimately, but could not find the words to describe it. When her therapist in those early months had asked her to talk about that night, Layla had opened her mouth and found nothing there—no language, no narrative, only a kind of blank horror.

Three years of this had worn her down. She was sleeping poorly, eating little, and had withdrawn from nearly all of her friendships. Her mother called regularly from the old neighborhood, worried, but Layla could not bear to hear the concern in her voice. She had come to therapy now because her doctor had insisted, because she could feel herself slipping further away from the person she had once been, and because some small, desperate part of her wondered if there was any way back.
